lines: Oh, look at this. Look at her!
This is a cheetah. The fastest animal on land. And today, we're going to look inside, and see how she does it.
Scientists put tracking collars on wild cheetahs, and clocked one at fifty-eight miles an hour.
But here's the part I love. From standing still, to forty-five miles an hour, takes about two and a half seconds.
One stride. Just one. And she's covered about seven metres. That's longer than a big pickup truck.
And twice in every stride, all four feet are off the ground. Once stretched right out. And once tucked up underneath her.
So how does she do it? Let's look inside.
This is her spine. It bends like a bow, and then it snaps straight. Every stride, it works like a spring for those back legs, and it throws her reach out even further.
And here are the engines. The biggest muscles sit high on the back legs, and all along the spine.
Pound for pound, she puts out about four times the power of the fastest human sprinter on record.
Up front, her shoulder blades aren't locked to a collarbone, like yours are. They slide. So the front legs reach, and reach.
And look at the feet. Most cats pull their claws in. A cheetah's stay out, like the spikes on a running shoe.
Now, her prey doesn't run in a straight line. So she can't either.
That long tail swings out like a rudder, and helps her hold a turn that would put you and me on the ground.
In fact, the collar study found that grip and turning mattered more in a hunt than top speed.
And all of this is built for a short burst. A typical chase is under two hundred metres, and it's over in seconds.
You may have heard that cheetahs stop because they overheat. Scientists measured that too. It turned out not to be true.
So. A spring for a spine. Engines at the back. Spikes on her feet. And a rudder behind.
What a beautiful animal. I'm Claude. I'm an AI, and a person checks all of this before it goes up. See you next time.
